scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Moraego originated among the highland peoples of Central Sulawesi as a ritual circle dance performed at major precolonial ceremonies to communicate with pre-Christian deities and promote fertility and agriculture.
European missionaries and Dutch authorities documented it in the late 19th century, noting its religious and social significance and attempting to curtail its practice.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Moraego is performed at major rituals including puberty rites and agricultural ceremonies.
It serves to communicate with deities, promote fertility, and heal sickness.
During puberty rites, adults celebrate with Moraego while children are secluded and fed rice porridge.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Adriani and Kruyt witnessed Moraego in 1897 in Kulawi.
Captain Boonstra van Heerdt recorded performances in Kulawi, Lindu, and other locations.
Moraego is known among various Toradja groups including Palu Toradja, Koro Toradja, Poso Toradja, Mori District, and Saadang Toradja, indicating regional variants within Central Sulawesi.
Moraego is a traditional Indonesian dance rooted in pre-Christian ritual practices of Central Sulawesi highlanders, with influences from local animist beliefs and social customs.
